blocks.title: ABSTRACT
blocks.content:
This thesis explores a construction of the family of topological invariants
for certain oriented 3-manifolds based on the state-integral approach developed by
Andersen, Garoufalidis, and Kashaev in the Archimedean setting. Starting from an
ideal triangulation of a 3-manifold equipped with angle data, variables are assigned
to the faces and tetrahedra, taking values in a so-called ’Gaussian group’. The
invariant is defined by integrating a distribution defined from the combinatorics of
the triangulation and a special function over a product of the Gaussian group.

Motivation and Background

which draws together tools from quantum topology, Teichm¨uller theory, and aspects
of quantum group representation theory.

blocks.title: Connections to Representation Theory
blocks.content:
Connections to Representation Theory
Although harmonic analysis appears only peripherally in this work, the representa-
tion-theoretic context provides important background motivation. At a classical level,
the moduli space of flat G-connections on a 3-manifold (character variety) and the
boundary data in the state-integral may be interpreted as holonomy-type parameters
in this setting.
In the quantum case, the function Ψa,c has close connections to the representation
theory of quantum groups, including Uq(sl2), where it arises in the construction of
intertwiners and associators.

blocks.title: Foundational Definitions
blocks.content:
Foundational Definitions
Definition 1. A locally compact abelian group (LCA group) is a topological group L
satisfying:
1. Abelian structure: xy = yx for all x, y ∈L.
2. Local compactness: Every point x ∈L admits a neighborhood whose closure
is compact.
3. Hausdorff separation: Distinct points are separable via disjoint open sets.
The combination of commutativity and local compactness ensures the existence
of Haar measure and well-posed harmonic analysis.

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.content:
Examples
The class of LCA groups encompasses:
7
• Euclidean spaces Rn.
• The circle group T (written multiplicatively), central to Fourier series.
• Discrete groups such as Z, finite cyclic groups Z/nZ, and their countable direct
sums.
• Compact profinite groups, as inverse limits of finite abelian groups.
• Non-Archimedean fields such as Qp.
• Direct sums and products of LCA groups, which are also LCA groups. For
example, the group R × Z is an LCA group as both R and Z are LCA.

A homomorphism of LCA groups is a continuous group homomorphism between locally compact abelian groups. An isomorphism of LCA groups is a group isomorphism ϕ: L →H that is also a homeomorphism. In other words, it is a bijective continuous map whose inverse is also continuous.

Let L be a locally compact abelian (LCA) group, equipped with its topology as a topological group. A Pontryagin character on L is a continuous group homomorphism χ: L →T, where T = {z ∈C | |z| = 1} is the circle group with its standard topology. The set of all such characters forms the Pontryagin dual group bL := Homcont(L, T), which is itself a topological group when endowed with the compact-open topology—that is, the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets of L. This makes bL into an LCA group as well.

blocks.title: Angled Quantum Dilogarithm
blocks.content:
Angled Quantum Dilogarithm
To define the analytic weight functions that drive the state-integral invariant, we
now introduce an angle-deformed quantum dilogarithm Ψa,c derived from the primitive
function φ. This deformation encodes geometric data and satisfies a pentagon identity
modified by angle parameters, crucial for proving the topological invariance of the
state-integral under Pachner moves.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.content:
Remark
The analytic nature of the state-integral reflects a synthesis of:
• Combinatorial topology via ideal triangulations and face gluings;
• Harmonic analysis on self-dual Gaussian groups;
• Functional identities of the angled quantum dilogarithm Ψa,c, including the
pentagon relation;
• Quantum holonomy representation theory via angle structures and boundary
data.
This aligns with frameworks developed in Garoufalidis–Kashaev and Andersen–
Kashaev, and elucidates the role of quantum deformation parameters in determining
the analytic and distributional nature of the state-integral.

C = c R× × R× denotes the coefficient system arising from the Gaussian group, reflecting the multiplicative harmonic analysis used in defining the model. The target space H1(∂M; C) parametrizes generalized boundary holonomies: that is, values of the angle structure assigned to edges lying in the boundary torus. These data specify the “external” parameters for the quantum wavefunction defined by the state-integral.

Let C = c R× × R× be the self-dual Gaussian group used for the state variables. It acts (by pointwise multiplication) on the boundary edge chain group C1(∂X; Z). After we integrate out the internal face variables and impose the face–pairing constraints, the resulting tempered distribution is supported on assignments that satisfy the edge relations; hence it factors through edge homology: FF,M : A(∂X)2 −→H1(∂M; C) −→C. Each boundary component of M is a torus, so H1(∂M; Z) is free abelian. For a free abelian group F there is a canonical isomorphism F ⊗C ∼= Hom(F, C); hence H1(∂M; C) = H1(∂M) ⊗C

The condition H2(M; Z) = 0 is imposed for analytic reasons: it rules out closed normal surfaces that would cause squared Dirac δ-factors when the kine- matical kernel is multiplied by the pushed-forward dynamical content, see [1, Proof of Theorem 7] and [6]. It does not imply the existence of a globally balanced angle structure on any given triangulation.

The balancing condition requires that the angle sum around each internal edge equals (2, 1) ∈C. This enforces a discrete flatness condition—zero holonomy around internal edges—which is essential for gluing consistency. It parallels the kernel constraints in Andersen–Kashaev [1], where vanishing holonomy ensures the state- integral is a well-defined distribution.

It also ensures that the product of the kinematical kernel and the dynam- ical content defines a well-behaved distribution after integrating out the internal edge parameters. More precisely, it guarantees that the quantum operator algebra defined by the edge equations is non-degenerate, which is necessary for consistent gluing. This mirrors the analytic condition in the TQFT construction of Andersen–Kashaev [1], where a gluing distribution GY is well-defined only when certain operator combi- nations vanish.
